history.subject: Height of a tree
history.content: The depth of a tree is considered to be the maximum number of edges from the root to any leaf node correct? So for example if a tree consists of the root, the roots child, and the roots grandchild the depth would be 2. Also, would the height be 3 in this scenario?

You are correct about the depth part. Depth = 2

But the height of the tree is also 2

Note that Depth and height are originally defined for nodes.

  • The depth of a node is the number of edges from the root to the node
  • The height of a node is the number of edges from the node to the deepest leaf

So depth of root node = number of edges from root to <node=root> = 0
depth of child node = 1
depth of grandchild node = 2

height of root node = 2
height of child = 1
height of grandchild = 0

In the context of trees, we usually mean

Height of tree = number of edges from root to the deepest leaf , i.e. root -> child -> grandchild = 2
Depth of tree = Depth of deepest node = Depth of grandchild node, i.e. grandchild <- child <- root = 2

Here is a diagram that might help:

Depth of a tree is always same as its height. But that is not true for the other nodes. For other nodes it’s just flipped…goes from 0 onwards from top to bottom ( depth ) and goes from the maximum downwards from top to bottom for height

history.subject: Insertion in 2-3-4 and B-Trees
history.content: In a 2-3-4 tree, when inserting into a full node (one with 3 keys), should we split the node first—promoting the middle key to the parent—and then insert the new key into the appropriate child? Or should we first insert the new key into the node, creating a 4-key node, and then promote one of the keys? If it's the latter, which key should be promoted—the 2nd or 3rd—and does it matter? Does the same approach apply to B-trees?

You can do it both ways but I believe for the final review, the solution involves first inserting the new key and then promoting it. 

For 2-3-4 trees, you may promote either the 2nd or the 3rd.
As a general simplification, in code you might use

int index = (n + 1) / 2; // for median element

so usually this will round the number down to nearest int.

So, based on that logic, you can get the (4 + 1) / 2 = 2.5 => 2nd index

But remember to be consistent about your approach. If you need to split more than 1 time, use the same index, i.e. 2 or 3 based on what you chose.

<md>You can use StringBuilder to create the list of names with commas and then pre-loop to remove null, using something like this:

```java
class HelloWorld {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();

        String[] list = {"one", "two", null}; // Example with null in the list
        
        String tempSep = "";  //Temporary seperator value. We will modify this if a comma is needed between the strings.
        for (int i = 0; i < list.length; i++) {
            if (list[i] != null) {
                sb.append(tempSep).append(list[i]);
                tempSep = ", "; // This assignment will only occur if the loop runs for any length longer than 1, meaning that you won't have trailing commas.
            }
        }

        System.out.println("Output: " + sb.toString());
    }
}
```</md>
